• **Post‑game engine review** of every critical position to train pattern recognition. | | **2** | **Neglect of king safety (moving the king into danger or leaving it exposed).**
Examples: 27 Kg4?, 12…Kf8??, 33…Bxh3+ after 33 Re1??. | King‑side weaknesses are the most common cause of quick losses in bullet. | • **King‑safety checklist** before each move: Is my king on a safe square? Have I just opened a line to it?
• **Practice “defensive mode”** – play slower games where you only move the king when absolutely necessary.
• **Study classic king‑safety motifs** (e.g., back‑rank mates, smothered mates) to recognise them instantly. | | **3** | **Inaccurate piece placement / premature pawn pushes that create targets.**
Examples: 22…Ne5?, 27…Bf8??, 8…e5?! (first game). | Misplaced pieces lose material and give the opponent easy winning chances. | • **“One‑move‑look‑ahead” habit:** after moving a piece, verify that it cannot be captured by a lower‑valued piece.
• **Opening‑repertoire refinement:** stick to lines you know well; avoid speculative pawn advances (like …e5 in the Bird) unless you have calculated the consequences.
• **Endgame‑style evaluation** even in the middlegame – ask “Is this pawn structure healthy? Do I have a good outpost for my knights?” | --- ### Bottom line The PGN belongs to **Grandmaster X**. The decisive moments were usually a single tactical blunder (often involving the king) or an inaccurate piece placement.
